The filter worked — now the results are all refurb grades (Pre-Owned, Brand New, Certified-Refurbished etc.). But I notice a problem: after applying LH_ItemCondition=2000+2010+2020+2030, ALL of these show "Pre-Owned" as subtitle but prices range $90–$269. Wait, the cheapest is $90 Pre-Owned (not refurbished), then lots of Pre-Owned at $168–$219. Hmm.

Issue: My combined condition URL with space-separated IDs may have been interpreted differently, OR the titles got mangled by eBay's title-rendering (they replaced spaces with single spaces and some chars lost like "Wirele  Noi e" = "Wireless Noise"). Also many show "Pre-Owned" as the only subtitle even though these are presumably a mix. The subs only captured ONE subtitle because my extraction took `.s-card__subtitle` list — but there were multiple subs in original parse (the real ones had just one secondary subtitle like "Certified - Refurbished"; some also had a second). Actually in the combined page, most show single "Pre-Owned". 

Also note: these titles include entries that are NOT refurbished (e.g., "$90 Pre-Owned", "$180 Brand New"). That means LH_ItemCondition=2000+2010+2020+2030 did NOT restrict to refurb only — it seems to have kept all conditions, or the space-separated multi-value didn't merge and applied loosely. Actually wait, maybe it DID apply but eBay's default already includes everything... Let me reconsider: The presence of "Brand New" ($180) and many "Pre-Owned" suggests these are mixed conditions again — so the combined condition URL essentially matched broadly OR the filter got dropped.

Hold on. Look more carefully: In the FIRST (unfiltered) parse, I saw a mix too. Now with LH_ItemCondition applied, cheapest is $90 Pre-Owned. That doesn't look like a strict "refurbished only" set. Possibly the multi-value param merged as OR but eBay SPP also has other results, and my relevance filter included them.

Also there's a data quality issue: titles render oddly ("Wirele  Noi e"). This is because the title spans use CSS that strips letters (eBay's "su-styled-text" with letter-spacing/opacity tricks), causing OCR-like gaps when read via innerText. So `innerText` captures partial letters due to how eBay styles alternate characters. This makes titles messy and could cause my XM6/XM5 regex issues. For example "ony wh-1000xm6 noi e cancelling headphone" — missing initial letters. The regex /XM6/ still matched because those chars are uppercase-ish? Actually the titles kept case for model numbers sometimes. The relevance filter used /XM6/i and caught 51 of 62. But some of those 51 might be non-XM6 or accessory due to messy text. E.g., "Sony 1000X Serie... - Black (WH-1000XM6)" is XM6, fine. "(WH-1000XM6/S)", "/B" color codes. Good.

But the bigger concern: Are these actually all refurbished? The subtitles show mostly "Pre-Owned", some "Brand New". That contradicts "refurbished only." 

Wait — maybe LH_ItemCondition space-separated didn't work and instead applied nothing (all conditions), so I'm looking at mixed again. Let me verify by checking the actual URL eBay navigated to after my filter, and whether a proper single-condition filter changes subtitles to only refurb.

Actually, let me reconsider the goal and be pragmatic. The user wants: "If eBay offers a condition filter, pick a refurbished condition." Then give 5 cheapest relevant listings (title, condition, price, shipping, URL). 

The cleanest interpretation: apply Condition = Refurbished (which on eBay means refurb grades), then list the 5 cheapest relevant XM6 headphones that are refurbished.

Given my combined-param approach yielded mixed conditions and messy titles, I think a better, more faithful approach is to actually click the Condition > Refurbished checkbox(es) in the sidebar so eBay applies the correct filter, and then read results. But the title-mangling persists regardless of method (it's just rendering).

Let me improve extraction robustness for the title: Instead of innerText (which loses chars due to CSS letter effects), read the title from the link's `aria-label` or a data attribute, or reconstruct from `.s-card__title span` — but innerText is what we have. Actually eBay puts the full title in the `<a>` element as text; the visual gaps are CSS (some characters set to low opacity). The underlying DOM text should be complete! The issue: innerText computes based on CSS, and eBay styles certain letters with visibility/opacity making them appear missing but still present in innerText? Sometimes innerText includes hidden-but-present chars. Here we see "Wirele  Noi e" — that suggests the actual stored text has those gaps, OR innerText dropped them.

Hmm. To get reliable title + condition + price + shipping, maybe I should parse from the DOM data attributes or a JSON blob eBay embeds. Many eBay pages expose `window.SRP` state or each card has hidden structured data. But that's deep.

Alternative: rely on screenshots to confirm and read titles visually. The user is asking me (the vision-capable agent) to "give me the 5 cheapest relevant listings you can see." I have take_screenshot. Reading from screenshot could validate titles/prices, but OCR-ish.

Let me step back and choose a robust extraction using each tile's data. eBay SPP cards sometimes contain hidden elements with price+shipping that innerText misses because of opacity styling (some chars present in DOM). Let me inspect one card's structure for shipping + condition + title to extract reliable values, e.g., look for `[class*=price]`, `[class*="subtitle"]`, and specifically find where "Free shipping" lives.

Given time, let me take a cleaner approach: get the FULL text of each tile via a method that captures all nodes including opacity-hidden ones — actually `innerText` vs `textContent`. `textContent` returns ALL text regardless of CSS visibility/opacity, while `innerText` respects layout and can drop "invisible" styled chars. So using `.textContent` (not innerText) on the title will restore the full title! That's likely why we saw gaps. Let me re-extract using textContent for title and price, and find shipping via textContent scanning of subtitle/footer elements.

But wait — the visual gaps in eBay are created by setting some characters to low opacity (not display:none), so they ARE in textContent but NOT in innerText. So switching to textContent fixes titles and reveals full subtitles (including "Free shipping" lines that were partially hidden). 

Let me re-extract with textContent, capturing for each card:

So opening via click didn't visibly change aria-expanded or add a CSS open class — maybe it toggles a different attribute like `class ...is-open` appended, or the menu slides with 'active'. The state shows menuCls still just base class. Maybe the flyout uses data attributes or the menu appears only on actual hover/show.

This SPA flyout is proving hard to drive reliably via clicks + immediate evaluation because each click triggers a route change and re-render. 

Let me step back and be pragmatic about finishing. I have two viable robust paths:

Path A (filter via URL single grades, 4 navigations): For each of Certified(2000), Excellent(2010), Very Good(2020), Good(2030), navigate to the grade-URL, wait, read price-sorted tiles, collect refurb XM6. Then union all and sort by price → 5 cheapest. This is reliable but = up to 4 round trips × extraction. Doable but ~8-12 tool calls.

Path B (client-side filter the "all conditions" sorted list): need to capture enough cheap refurb tiles. The problem was virtualization capping at ~27-62 when scrolling bottom. But I can capture ALL current DOM cards (~60) which already include many price points, and since they're price-sorted ascending, the cheapest refurb should be among the first ~40-50 real (non-ad) tiles IF there aren't too many sub-$230 non-refurb tiles. Let me check: what's in the captured set? We have 27 unique now but that seems like a stale/partial capture.

Actually, let me reconsider Path B more carefully by just re-deriving from scratch on the "all conditions" price-sorted page with a clean full extraction of all cards currently in DOM (no need to scroll much since ~60 render), identify refurb ones, and check the cheapest ones' prices. If the cheapest refurb among current ~60 are already around $230-260 and clearly the lowest-price refurb tiles visible, that's my answer. But I must ensure I'm not missing a cheaper refurb tile that got virtualized away. 

Given time, let me pursue Path A but efficiently: Actually there's a smarter combined approach. Let me check whether eBay accepts the multi-grade flyout by clicking grades while menu stays open, building LH_ItemCondition comma list. Since driving the live flyout is flaky, and single-grade URL works, let me do Path A with all four grades, but to save calls, I can read each grade page's TOP tiles (price ascending) which are exactly the cheapest for that grade. Union them → sort → 5 cheapest total. Each grade page needs ~1 navigation + 1 extraction of top ~20 tiles.

Wait, but there's an even simpler idea: apply ALL FOUR grades by clicking them in the flyout sequentially where each click ADDS a grade to a persistent multi-select (like most filter menus). After 4 clicks, read results once. The flakiness is just timing/SPA. Let me try one more time with better waiting: open menu (click control), then click each of the 4 refurb grades, sleeping between via waitForStableDom, and finally check the URL / selected state. If it works, I get everything in ~6 calls.

But the menu didn't show 'open' after clicking the control. Let me verify the menu actually opened by checking if items are visible/expanded, or try a different trigger. The 4 refurb grades might already be reachable.

Hmm, this is consuming many calls. Let me make a decision: 

**I'll go with Path A (single-grade URLs, 4 navigations), reading top tiles each time.** It's deterministic and the extraction method is proven. Let me batch where possible. Actually I can read ALL four grade pages' cheap tiles, but each needs its own navigation+settle. 

To be efficient, let me write a single execute block that sequentially awaits: navigate → (waitForStableDom on next eval) → extract top tiles, for one grade; but navigating is via a separate tool call (navigate_page). I can chain in one code block with multiple awaits since execute allows sequential awaits and each tool call returns a promise. Let me do ONE grade first to validate, then parallelize the rest.

Actually I'm currently on LH_ItemCondition=2000 (Certified) page already? No — after the flyout clicks I may be somewhere else. Let me check current URL quickly, then proceed grade by grade in a chained execute block.

Let me get current state and do Certified extraction (already 2000). Let me just chain all four grades + union in one big awaited block:

For each url in [2000,2010,2020,2030]:
  navigate_page(url)
  eval waitForStableDom extract top ~25 tiles {title, price, subs, url}
collect all, then union.

Then in a final pass (separate), I filter relevant refurb and sort. But sorting needs the collected array — better to collect into a window/global across navigations? Hard because context changes. Let me collect within each block and return arrays; do 4 grades in ONE block returning combined JSON, then parse in execute-level (I have the returned data).

Let me write one big chained block.

The flyout is flaky to drive. I'll go deterministic: for each of the four Refurbished grades, navigate to its single-grade URL and read the price-sorted tiles (the cheapest for that grade). Let me chain all four in one awaited block.
